changes.text: Windows installation no longer fails when opening the installer dialogs or when an existing Hub executable does not need to be replaced.
Hub self-updates preserve existing desktop and Start menu shortcuts without creating additional shortcuts or restoring shortcuts you removed.
When the Hub icon changes, Hub asks Windows to refresh its icon cache and existing Hub shortcuts once for the signed-in user. Updates with the same icon do not repeat the refresh.
Disabling automatic updates stops background checks and downloads for the corresponding product. Manual update checks remain available.
Hub windows, the app bundle, Windows shortcuts, the taskbar, the system tray, and the installer use the refreshed Hub icon.
Hub windows, the app bundle, Windows shortcuts, the taskbar, and the system tray use the new white icon on a black background.
The quick SDK change menu lists newer versions first, with separators between upgrades, the installed version, and older versions. Sources with the same SDK version list newer Studio versions first.
Successful SDK installation and update results are highlighted in green.
Restored the blue H icon for Hub windows, the app bundle, Windows shortcuts, the taskbar, and the system tray.

Unity SDK checks recognize equivalent text across UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32, and common legacy encodings, including BOM and line-ending conversions. Encoding-only differences are listed as Review recommended without blocking updates, and equivalent read-only files retain their existing bytes.
Hub uses the refreshed light application icon for its windows, app bundle, Windows shortcuts, taskbar, and system tray.

Unity SDK checks and updates recognize LF, CRLF, and mixed line endings as unchanged text, including conversions after an update, avoiding false modification warnings and unnecessary write-access checks. Binary files and actual content changes remain strictly checked.
Missing Unity SDK documentation and samples are reported separately and no longer fail SDK verification or block updates. Required SDK files retain their integrity and write-protection checks.

SDK check logs retain the file list and count for line-ending-only differences. Non-blocking items are labeled Review recommended. The SDK status shows normal for unchanged files, line-ending-only differences, and missing documentation or samples, with details kept in the check log.
Integration-list tooltips show only the SDK installation path. Version tooltips appear only when a newer local SDK is available and show its version number.
Engine Integrations shows the installed SDK version and file status. The quick-change menu lists local SDK versions and identifies the current source.
SDK changes keep safety checks, confirmation, progress, and results in one window, with clear downgrade warnings and separate lists of modified and missing files.

SDK updates, repairs, and removal check write protection before confirmation and again before changing files. Failures highlight read-only or inaccessible files and explain how to restore write access.
Automatic SDK scans run quietly in the background. Local SDK choices refresh after Studio installation and when opening the source menus.
SDK operation windows show a red engine-running warning only when the target project is open. Unity integration reports open as text files stored in Hub's application-data folder.

Integration menus distinguish full SDK and project-association management from quick SDK changes. Project columns offer clearly named folder actions, including right-click access, and SDK status tooltips label the installation path.
Project-association guidance explains that each Harken project and game project can belong to only one local association.
Double-clicking a Studio version preselects that version when creating a new project.
Hub uses the updated application icon for its windows, app bundle, Windows shortcuts, taskbar, and system tray.

Unity SDK management no longer reports that a closed project is still open because of a leftover lock file. SDK checks, installation, updates, removal, moves, and recovery can proceed once the project is no longer in use.
When Hub cannot check whether a Unity project is in use, it reports the access error and affected path instead of claiming that Unity is running.

Click the Project, Last Opened, or Version column header to sort the project list in ascending or descending order. Engine Integrations supports the same sorting for the HARKEN Project and Game Project columns. Each page remembers its sorting preference.
The project list shows minutes since the last launch, adds hours after one hour, and adds days after 24 hours instead of using vague labels such as Yesterday.
Unity SDK verification reports separately how many files differ from their contents at installation, are missing, or cannot be read, with guidance for each problem.

Studio installations retain recovery information if saving the installation record fails, and Hub checks interrupted installations on startup. Installations in progress are no longer shown as damaged. If recovery needs administrator access, choose Repair in Versions.
Studio repair checks for running programs in the installation folder before replacing files and explains which programs need to be closed.
Hub update installers are kept separately from temporary Studio installation files so Studio cleanup cannot remove a pending Hub update.

Unity SDK management no longer treats normal embedded-package records as dependency conflicts. Genuine dependency restrictions use neutral text, and successful SDK verification is shown in green in both languages.

SDK file replacement failures show the affected paths and system error, with guidance for write protection, permissions, files in use, and version-control checkout when applicable. Related Hub prompts and log messages support Chinese and English.
Unreal SDK checks detect missing, unreadable, or empty native libraries and core headers for the current platform before installation and when verifying an installed SDK.

With a Studio build that supports the new checks, project upgrades detect existing files that cannot be written before changing project data. Hub lists the affected files and explains how to restore write access.

On Windows, new installations default to HarkenStudioHub directly under Program Files, and the main application and setup use the HarkenStudioHub name. Existing installation locations and older Studio launchers remain supported.
Windows desktop shortcuts and taskbar icons now display the H logo with crisp images for different icon sizes.
Project association prompts in Engine Integrations now refer only to Unity projects.
Hub uses the gradient Harken Studio logo and matching H window and tray icons, and consistently displays Harken Studio Hub in menus, notifications, dialogs, and installer details.
Hub displays the Harken Studio logo above a separate Hub label, updates its window title and repository link, and removes the previous application icon.
Project format incompatibility messages show the selected Studio version and the project and Studio Schema versions from the compatibility check.
Hub and Studio updates preserve each other's progress when running together, and outdated operations cannot overwrite newer update state.
Manual and background Studio downloads can run together. Packages remain protected from competing downloads and cache cleanup until installation handoff finishes.
Updates and local build checks recover from temporary file locks on Windows without reporting unsaved state as complete.
Studio installation, repair, and removal recover when Windows briefly locks the installation index.
Reopening a project in a compatible Studio version activates its existing window, and Hub recognizes a successful handoff.
Choose SDKs bundled with installed Studio versions directly from the SDK source dropdown. Click anywhere in the field to open the list, or browse for another folder.

SDK checks show version changes and file counts grouped by addition, update, removal, and preservation. Preserved files are collapsed, and a separate check log highlights failures, warnings, and recommended actions.
New Studio installations use shorter folder names without lengthy build identifiers. Different builds of the same version can still be installed side by side.
Windows now displays the application name without an additional description.
Engine Integrations uses system file and folder pickers, restoring address-bar path navigation on Windows.
Hub and Studio updates now use the new GitHub repository, with COS downloads retained as a fallback.
SDK integration retries temporary file locks on Windows instead of failing immediately.
Unreal SDK installation now rejects incomplete native headers before changing the game project.
